page5_img_1.png.title: Bounds on transitive-fault rates by aggregation interval for Apache, MySQL, and Perl
page5_img_1.png.description: A table of lower–upper bound ranges for network transitive-fault rates (fraction of directed 2‑paths that could spuriously imply information flow) computed for five aggregation intervals: Hourly, Daily, Monthly, Yearly and Lifespan. Values are shown separately for Apache, MySQL and Perl; for example, Hourly faults are 0.48–0.55 (Apache), 0.38–0.43 (MySQL), and 0.45–0.52 (Perl), while Yearly faults are 0.11–0.49 (Apache), 0.37–0.50 (MySQL), and 0.17–0.50 (Perl). The upper bounds are consistently near 0.5 across projects and intervals (worst case ≈50%), whereas the lower bounds tend to decrease as the aggregation window grows (most notably for Apache), indicating that longer aggregations can reduce the optimistic estimate of transitive faults; MySQL’s lower bound remains relatively stable across intervals. The ranges reflect the paper’s optimistic and pessimistic labeling of 2‑paths (lower = optimistic, upper = pessimistic).

page2_img_1.png.title: Temporal order determines transitive information flow in A→B→C reply chains
page2_img_1.png.description: The figure shows three nodes A, B, C with directed edges A→B (labeled t1) and B→C (labeled t2). Two small schematics to the right illustrate that if t1 < t2 then information can validly flow from A to C via B, but if t1 > t2 the A→B→C topology cannot support A→C flow (the transitive link is crossed out). The diagram emphasizes that identical topologies can imply different information flows depending on message timestamps, illustrating the paper’s point about transitive faults introduced by temporal aggregation of email replies.

page6_img_1.png.title: Spearman correlations of 2‑path ranking across aggregation intervals (Apache, MySQL, Perl)
page6_img_1.png.description: Table of Spearman rank correlations (with p‑values) comparing node orderings by number of 2‑paths with versus without transitive faults, for aggregation intervals of 1 day, 5 days and 1 year. Correlations increase with longer aggregation windows: Apache rises from 0.67 (p=0.01) at 1 day to 0.82 (p=0.0001) at 1 year; MySQL from 0.52 (p=0.22) to 0.73 (p=0.0001); Perl from 0.74 (p=0.01) to 0.86 (p=0.0001). Most correlations are statistically significant (p≤0.01), except MySQL at the 1‑day interval (p=0.22), indicating that short aggregation windows—especially for sparser projects—can reduce stability of the 2‑path ranking.

page3_img_1.png.title: Observed vs. unobserved information flow among A, B, and C
page3_img_1.png.description: The schematic shows three circular nodes labeled A, B, and C. A solid curved arrow from B to A, annotated "Observed Communication," represents an observed reply (evidence of information flowing from B to A). Two dashed arrows, annotated "Unobserved Information Flow," run from A to B and from B to C, indicating potential reading-only or otherwise unrecorded flows (A→B and B→C) that the reply-to network would not capture, illustrating how observed reply edges can miss true information paths and produce incomplete network views.

page6_img_2.png.title: Edges added by ER, PA, and TW missing-link models for Apache, MySQL, and Perl
page6_img_2.png.description: The table gives the total number of edges inserted into each project’s reply-to network when simulating missing links under three models: ER (Erdős–Rényi), PA (Preferential Attachment), and TW (Time Window). For Apache the added-edge counts are ER=26,555, PA=28,326, TW=29,032; for MySQL ER=4,917, PA=4,752, TW=5,362; for Perl ER=40,350, PA=40,122, TW=37,910. These augmentations are several times larger than the original edge counts reported in the paper (Apache 11,227; MySQL 1,989; Perl 16,026), i.e., roughly 2.3–2.7× the original number of edges. TW produced the most edges for Apache and MySQL, while ER produced the most for Perl, showing that all three models add substantial numbers of plausible "missing" links for the robustness experiments.

page7_img_1.png.title: Transitive-fault rate vs aggregation interval for Apache, Perl, MySQL
page7_img_1.png.description: Three side-by-side scatter plots report transitive-fault rates (y-axis) against aggregation interval in hours (x-axis, 1–10,000) for (a) Apache, (b) Perl and (c) MySQL. Each plot shows a pessimistic/upper bound (red circles) and an optimistic/lower bound (blue crosses); the upper bound stays near ≈0.5–0.55 across all interval sizes, whereas the lower bound drops rapidly as the aggregation window increases for Apache and Perl (from ≈0.45–0.5 down to ≈0.1–0.17) but remains relatively high and flat for MySQL (≈0.4 to ≈0.35). The figure thus illustrates that worst-case inferred transitive faults can approach 50% at fine temporal granularity, but increasing the aggregation interval reduces the optimistic fault estimate and both bounds stabilize over multi-month to year-long windows, with MySQL’s higher lower-bound reflecting its sparser, shorter exchanges described in the paper.
